passage:
Elif had not spoken to Rafael all morning, and the Porto flat felt smaller because of it. At lunch she finally set down her fork. "Three years we lived here. I covered your rent when you lost the café job. And now you just leave me for Berlin."
Rafael felt the familiar tug in his chest. He made himself ask the question slowly, in his head: did I actually wrong her? He had told her in March, two months early, as their flat agreement said. He had paid back the café months by summer. The answer was no.
"I'm grateful for that rent, truly," he said. "And I'm still going. I'll help you find someone good for my room, and I'll call on Sundays."
Elif's eyes filled. "It won't be the same."
"No," he said gently. "It won't. I'll miss this too."
That evening they wrote the room advert together, arguing over whether to mention the noisy tram.

qa.q: When had Rafael told Elif about moving?
qa.a: Rafael told her in March, two months early, as their flat agreement said.

qa.q: What was Rafael feeling when Elif mentioned the rent she had covered?
qa.a: He felt a familiar tug of guilt in his chest, pulled between gratitude and the urge to give in.

qa.q: What turning point let Rafael keep his decision?
qa.a: Slowly asking himself whether he had actually wronged Elif, and checking the facts, showed the answer was no, so he could stay kind without changing his plan.

qa.q: How does Elif experience Rafael's calm answer?
qa.a: She still feels sad that it won't be the same, but being thanked and helped with the room lets her grieve the change instead of fighting it.

grounding: A young man checks whether he really wronged Elif, finds he did not, and keeps his move abroad while showing care in words and practical help.

"Seriously, Baljeet? After I stayed till midnight for your audit in March?" Sunaina dropped the shift roster on his desk in the hospital billing office. "Everyone always leaves me holding everything."
Baljeet's first instinct was to say fine, he would work Saturday. Instead he pulled up the roster history on his screen. He had covered for Sunaina twice since March. Saturday was his sister's graduation, marked on the leave calendar six weeks ago.
But one thing was true. Last Friday he had left without handing over the insurance files, and Sunaina had spent her evening finding them.
"You're right about Friday," he said. "That was my mistake, and I'm sorry. It won't happen again. Saturday I can't do. I can take your Tuesday late shift instead, if that helps."
Sunaina folded her arms, then unfolded them. "Tuesday helps," she muttered.
He wrote a note in his planner: handover checklist, every Friday.

qa.q: Where does the scene take place?
qa.a: It takes place in the hospital billing office.

qa.q: Why did Baljeet check the roster history before answering?
qa.a: He felt the pull to give in and wanted to know whether he had really wronged Sunaina or was only being pressured.

qa.q: Which part of Baljeet's reply worked, and why?
qa.a: He apologised plainly for the real mistake on Friday but kept his Saturday leave and offered the Tuesday shift, which showed care without giving in to pressure.

qa.q: How might Sunaina feel when her Friday complaint is admitted?
qa.a: She likely feels heard and less alone, which is why her folded arms loosen and she accepts the Tuesday offer.

grounding: A young man separates one real lapse, which he apologises for, from pressure to give up his leave, and keeps his decision while offering care.
